alt: Two words, home and house, drawn as two-layer blocks. Both share the denotation “a place where a person lives”; home adds a connotation layer of warmth, safety and belonging, while house carries little of that feeling.
caption: Words that share a literal meaning can carry very different feelings.

alt: Five words for a person careful with money arranged from admiring to critical: thrifty, frugal, economical, cheap and stingy. A table gives neutral, positive and negative versions of walk, determined, unusual, crowd and old.
caption: Same denotation, different connotation: the word decides whether readers admire or disapprove.

after: ## How connotation builds tone and style
alt: Four steps for analysing word choice: pick out significant words, name the connotation, compare with alternatives, and link the choice to tone and purpose. Below, tone (a gathering of residents or a mob of agitators) and style (endeavour and commence or try and start).
caption: Name the connotation, compare it with an alternative, then link it to tone and purpose.

alt: Douglass pairs three flattering phrases with harsh ones: your celebration with a sham, your boasted liberty with an unholy license, and your national greatness with swelling vanity. Notes explain the connotations of “boasted”, “unholy license” and “swelling”.
caption: Douglass attaches negative connotations to his audience’s proudest words.

after: ## Worked example 1: choosing connotation for an audience
alt: The draft “Students want to get out of school at lunch” is marked for “want” (mere desire) and “get out of” (escape). The revision “Students ask for the responsibility of leaving the grounds at lunchtime” is marked for polite “ask for”, “responsibility” as an obligation and neutral “leaving the grounds”.
caption: Choose words whose associations fit the audience, and make sure the evidence earns them.

after: ## Worked example 2: analysing connotation in a passage
alt: Six words from the orchard passage set against neutral alternatives with their connotations: swarmed (arrived) suggests invasion; machines (equipment) is impersonal; tearing out (removing) suggests violence; stood (grown) gives the trees dignity; quiet hillside suggests peace; scar of mud (cleared) suggests a wound.
caption: Comparing loaded words with neutral ones reveals the writer’s attitude.
